Apollo 11. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first human to set foot on the Moon. As he stepped onto the lunar surface, he spoke words that would become the century's most iconic utterance: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

NASA's Apollo 11 mission had carried three astronauts to the Moon. Neil Armstrong was the command pilot, Buzz Aldrin was the lunar module pilot, and Michael Collins piloted the command module Columbia, which remained in lunar orbit. Armstrong and Aldrin descended to the lunar surface in the lunar module Eagle, while Collins orbited above, spending the mission in the command module alone.

Buzz Aldrin was the second person to walk on the Moon, following Armstrong minutes later. The two spent about two hours and 31 minutes on the surface, collecting 47 pounds of moon rocks. The mission validated the lunar orbit rendezvous technique—undocking the landing module from the main spacecraft—proving the approach for future landings. The spacecraft launched from Kennedy Space Center atop a Saturn V rocket.

The mission was completed just before the decade's end, fulfilling President John F. Kennedy's 1961 pledge to land on the Moon before 1970. Apollo 11 stands as humanity's most celebrated moment of space exploration, forever marking our first steps beyond Earth.
